geometry.label: Room Length
geometry.rationale: Bedroom floor area affects the balance between spacious comfort and cosy enclosure. Bedrooms are typically smaller than living rooms; the narrower range reflects residential norms.

geometry.label: Room Width
geometry.rationale: Width constrains furniture layout and, at low values, produces a corridor-like enclosure effect that can increase perceived confinement.

geometry.label: Ceiling Height
geometry.construct: perceived openness / abstract cognition / cocoon effect
geometry.rationale: Ceiling height in bedrooms interacts with the dual desire for openness and cosy enclosure. Lower ceilings may increase the restorative cocoon effect for some participants; higher ceilings prime expansive thinking. Default 2.6 m is slightly lower than the living room to reflect typical residential proportions.

geometry.label: En-suite Door Present
geometry.construct: spatial connectivity / perceived convenience / privacy gradient
geometry.rationale: An en-suite door changes the spatial narrative of the room (private retreat with attached bathroom vs. standalone bedroom) and alters the wall composition and wayfinding affordances.

windows.label: Number of Windows
windows.construct: daylight access / morning light / circadian entrainment
windows.rationale: Bedroom window count affects morning daylight exposure, a primary circadian zeitgeber. One window is the residential norm; more windows increase circadian-entraining light exposure but may reduce perceived privacy.
windows.citation: Münch et al. (2020); Viola et al. (2008)

windows.label: Window-to-Wall Ratio
windows.construct: daylight factor / morning circadian light dose
windows.rationale: Bedroom glazing ratios are typically smaller than living rooms to support sleep privacy. The narrower range (0.08–0.25) reflects residential bedroom norms.

windows.label: Window Sill Height
windows.rationale: Higher sills provide privacy when lying in bed while still admitting daylight. Lower sills allow views while lying down but reduce privacy.

windows.label: Window Treatment
windows.construct: sleep environment quality / light-at-night suppression / morning light control
windows.rationale: Blackout curtains are the recommended default for bedrooms because light-at-night suppresses melatonin and disrupts sleep. The option to compare blackout vs. sheer conditions is a direct sleep-hygiene manipulation.
windows.citation: Viola et al. (2008); Chang & Chen (2005); Exelmans & Van den Bulck (2015)

windows.label: Exterior View Type
windows.rationale: The first visual input after waking influences morning affect and the day's initial stress trajectory. Nature views support restorative waking.

doors.label: Number of Doors
doors.rationale: Bedrooms are expected to be highly private. A single door is the norm. Two doors (e.g., main entrance + en-suite or wardrobe alcove) introduce spatial complexity and affect perceived privacy.

doors.label: Door Style
doors.rationale: Mirrored wardrobe doors are prevalent in residential bedrooms and both increase perceived spatial depth and introduce self-reflection cues. Flush doors recede visually; paneled doors add architectural detail.

lighting.label: Daylight Intensity
lighting.construct: circadian entrainment / sleep-related comfort / morning alertness
lighting.rationale: Daylight in the bedroom context is primarily relevant to morning exposure (circadian zeitgeber) and daytime rest quality. Default 0.45 is slightly lower than the living room to reflect the bedroom's primarily low-light role.
lighting.citation: Münch et al. (2020); Viola et al. (2008)

lighting.label: Artificial Light Intensity
lighting.rationale: Evening artificial light above ~10 lux suppresses melatonin onset. Lower artificial light intensity is preferred in bedroom contexts to support sleep preparation. Default 0.25 represents dim evening lighting.

lighting.label: Light Color Temperature
lighting.rationale: Cool light (>4000 K, high melanopic content) strongly suppresses melatonin and increases alertness—counterproductive in a bedroom. The range is restricted to 1800–4000 K to model plausible bedroom lighting conditions. Default 2700 K is warm candlelight-equivalent, optimal for pre-sleep environments.
lighting.citation: Chang & Chen (2005); Viola et al. (2008); Münch et al. (2020)

lighting.label: Primary Light Source Type
lighting.construct: light distribution / perceived intimacy / sleep-environment quality
lighting.rationale: Bedside lamps provide localised, low-level light suitable for reading without broadly illuminating the room. Overhead light raises the general illumination level and is less appropriate for pre-sleep conditions.

lighting.label: Night Light Present
lighting.construct: light-at-night / fear of dark / sleep quality
lighting.rationale: Nightlights provide orientation and safety during night waking but constitute light-at-night exposure. Their presence is a meaningful sleep-hygiene variable, particularly in studies of children, older adults, or anxiety.

materials.label: Wall Colour Hue
materials.construct: colour valence / arousal / sleep environment quality
materials.rationale: Blue-grey tones (around 210°) are associated with lower arousal and are commonly recommended for sleep environments. The full hue range is exposed to allow testing of competing hypotheses (e.g., whether warm bedroom colours increase comfort or arousal).

materials.label: Wall Colour Saturation
materials.construct: arousal / visual fatigue in a rest environment
materials.rationale: Bedroom saturation range is narrower than living room (cap at 0.30) because high-saturation bedrooms are unusual and would be confounded with deliberate over-stimulation. Default 0.06 is a muted, residential level.

materials.label: Wall Colour Lightness
materials.construct: perceived brightness / cosy enclosure vs. openness
materials.rationale: Slightly darker walls (lower value) can increase the cosy, enclosed character of a bedroom. Default 0.80 is lighter than a typical dark accent bedroom but darker than the living room default.

materials.label: Floor Material
materials.construct: warmth / softness / acoustic comfort / tactile comfort
materials.rationale: Carpet is the dominant bedroom floor choice because it provides tactile warmth for bare feet and acoustic softness. Default is soft carpet, which is the most strongly restorative option for a bedroom.

materials.label: Ceiling Material
materials.rationale: Bedroom ceilings are typically plain to minimise visual stimulation and maximise perceived room height. Textured ceilings add low-level visual complexity.

furniture.label: Bed Size
furniture.construct: perceived luxury / comfort affordance / spaciousness trade-off
furniture.rationale: Bed size signals the comfort level and social context of the bedroom (solo vs. couples). Larger beds occupy more floor space, reducing perceived spaciousness but increasing perceived luxury and comfort.

furniture.label: Bed Scale Factor
furniture.rationale: A continuous scale factor applied on top of the categorical bed_size, allowing fine-grained manipulation of how the bed dominates the room. Used in the current v1 implementation.

furniture.label: Mattress/Bedding Quality
furniture.construct: perceived comfort / socioeconomic status cue / restorative affordance
furniture.rationale: Visible bedding quality communicates the restorative affordance of the bed and the socioeconomic context of the room. Luxury bedding (layered, high-thread-count appearance) is associated with hotel-quality rest environments.

furniture.label: Pillow Count
furniture.construct: softness cue / perceived comfort / occupancy signal
furniture.rationale: Pillow count is a visible softness cue and signals the number of intended occupants. More pillows are associated with higher perceived comfort and hospitality.

furniture.label: Bedding Colour Tone
furniture.construct: warmth perception / colour valence / visual complexity of dominant object
furniture.rationale: The bed is the dominant object in a bedroom; its colour tone shapes the overall warmth character of the room independently of wall colour. This allows decoupling of wall hue and bedding hue as experimental variables.

furniture.label: Desk Present
furniture.construct: work intrusion / sleep hygiene / boundary violation
furniture.rationale: A desk in the bedroom violates the sleep-hygiene principle of stimulus control—the bed should be associated exclusively with sleep. Work reminders in the bedroom are associated with pre-sleep cognitive arousal and impaired sleep onset.

furniture.label: Television Present
furniture.construct: pre-sleep arousal / stimulus control violation / light-at-night
furniture.rationale: Bedroom televisions are associated with later sleep onset, shorter sleep duration, and poorer sleep quality. They violate stimulus-control principles and introduce light-at-night. Default is false (recommended sleep hygiene).
furniture.citation: Exelmans & Van den Bulck (2015); Chang & Chen (2005)

furniture.label: Furniture Density
furniture.construct: cognitive load / clutter / perceived spaciousness / restfulness
furniture.rationale: Bedroom furniture density affects perceived spaciousness and restfulness. Unlike the living room, where social density may be desirable, bedroom density is more uniformly linked to clutter-related stress at higher values.

furniture.label: Nightstand Count
furniture.construct: occupancy signal / social context / functional affordance
furniture.rationale: Nightstand count signals single (0–1) versus couples (2) occupancy, which affects perceived social context and may influence social belonging or loneliness judgements in experimental contexts.

furniture.label: Wardrobe Style
furniture.rationale: Wardrobes are large furniture pieces that dominate the wall composition of a bedroom. Mirrored versions increase perceived depth and introduce self-reflection. Freestanding wooden wardrobes add visual warmth and texture.

furniture.label: Clutter Level
furniture.construct: cognitive load / pre-sleep stress / sleep inhibition
furniture.rationale: Bedroom clutter is specifically linked to sleep quality impairment via chronic stress activation and reduced perceived sanctuary quality. Default is lower than the living room to reflect the bedroom's role as a primary restoration space.

plants.label: Plant Count
plants.construct: biophilic connection / air quality perception / restoration
plants.rationale: Biophilic benefit of plants is established (Kaplan, 1995), but bedroom-specific research is more equivocal — some sources caution against CO2 accumulation from many large plants in a closed sleeping space. Default is 0; the variable is included to allow experimental comparison.

plants.label: Plant Size
plants.rationale: Bedroom plants are typically smaller than living room plants. Floor-standing plants in a bedroom may feel intrusive or reduce navigable space. Tabletop-small is the most plausible bedroom form.

plants.label: Plant Species Type
plants.rationale: Succulent geometric forms are the most common bedroom plant choice, require minimal maintenance, and provide low-complexity organic form. Tropical leafy plants provide higher complexity but larger scale.

decoration.label: Painting / Art Count
decoration.construct: visual complexity / identity signalling / aesthetic preference
decoration.rationale: Bedroom art is typically more restrained than in living rooms. One to two pieces is the residential norm; more than three begins to feel overstimulating for a rest environment.

decoration.label: Painting Style
decoration.rationale: Nature landscapes are recommended for bedroom contexts because they support attention restoration and are associated with positive affect on waking. Abstract-calm pieces avoid the social presence introduced by figurative portraits, which may interfere with privacy in a bedroom.

decoration.label: Decoration Density
decoration.rationale: Bedroom decoration density is capped lower than the living room (0.50 vs. 1.0) because bedroom environments benefit from visual quiet to support sleep and restoration. High decoration density in a bedroom is specifically associated with stress and sleep disruption.

decoration.label: Rug Present
decoration.construct: warmth / softness cue / tactile comfort on waking
decoration.rationale: A rug beside the bed provides a softness and warmth cue for the first physical contact on waking. In combination with floor_material, it decouples the general floor character from the immediate waking tactile experience.
